# Projective contact weights: exact representations and a label-preserving obstruction

This note tests one precise bridge from projective boundary potentials to the ordinary lower-dimensional contact body. There is an exact fiberwise cone-volume representation and a class of inverse-power densities stable under continuous marginalization. There is also an actual obstruction to representing the weighted masses as uniform intrinsic volumes of any compatible convex family at the original lattice labels. No generalized mixed center theorem is proposed.

The unweighted full contact face and its lattice-preserving flattening are in `candidate 79217d237564c41f`. The simultaneous ordinary boundary potential is in `candidate 2d9458b5433d0a83`. Neither source asserts the weighted representation falsified below.

## 1. The common face, its labels and the projective chart

Let C be an actual compact convex body with lattice base coordinates z and continuous coordinates x in R^d. Fix a unit continuous normal u and an affine support h(z) with u·x≤h(z) on C. Write F_z for its contact faces, and restrict to the bases at which these have positive (d−1)-volume. As in the archived face theorem, rotating x and subtracting h(z) in the normal coordinate flattens the full common face by a lattice-preserving affine map. The resulting body has coordinates (z,ξ), ξ in R^m, m=d−1, and keeps the intrinsic fiber measure dξ exactly.

Assume on this face that H(z)>0 is affine and

    L(z,ξ)>0

is affine. The boundary weight of interest is the actual measure

    dν_z(ξ)=H(z)L(z,ξ)^(−d) dξ on F_z.                 (1)

All positivity assertions can be taken on the compact full face, so there are common positive lower bounds. H can arise as h(z)−u·y(z) for an affine source graph y(z); no centering of all the other fibers is needed in the algebra below.

Homogenization itself keeps the labels: the fiber z has the labeled linear plane

    Z=t z

in coordinates (Z,X,t). But the common linear change defining the chart L=1+a·x+b·z is

    (Z,X,t) ↦ (Z,X,τ),   τ=t+a·X+b·Z.

After τ=1, its ordinary projective image has base

    z'=z/L(z,x).                                       (2)

Equivalently the original labeled plane becomes Z=z(τ−a·X−b·Z). It is not in general a fixed-base plane Z=τz. When a varies in a continuous fiber, even its image base need not be constant. When a=0 the base can still be a nonintegral fractional-linear image. The full ordinary Jacobian is L^(−n−d−1), not a mixed measure Jacobian obtained by leaving the discrete labels untouched. We will not apply this change of chart to the lattice.

## 2. Exact fiberwise surface and cone-volume Jacobians

Fix a fiber, and use an apex y_z below its face, of height H=H(z)>0. Write points on the face relative to this apex as

    v=ξ+H u,     ξ⊥u,
    L=s+a_T·ξ,

where a_T is tangent to the face. Suppose the same denominator is positive also at the apex, as holds if the apex lies in C and the chart is positive on C. The fiberwise fractional map is v↦v/L. Its face image lies in the plane

    (s u+H a_T)·v'=H.

Put N=s u+H a_T. The exact tangential area Jacobian is

    dH_m(v')=|N| L^(−d) dH_m(v).                       (3)

For example, this follows by taking the norm of the exterior product of the m derivative vectors of v/L. Their normal is N, and the determinant expansion gives the factor L^(−m−1). The same formula follows from the full projective cofactor restricted to the original unit normal. N cannot vanish: if a_T=0, positivity on the face gives s>0.

The image support distance from the apex is H/|N|. Consequently (1) pushes forward EXACTLY as

    H L^(−d) dH_m(v) = (H/|N|) dH_m(v').              (4)

Thus it is cone-volume measure, not in general intrinsic area measure. If P_z=conv(y_z,F_z) and P'_z is its fiberwise projective image translated to put the apex at zero, radial integration gives

    ν_z(F_z)=d |P'_z|.                                (5)

The same identity holds on measurable patches as volume of the corresponding rays. Positivity of the chart makes each P'_z an actual bounded convex pyramid. This is a fiberwise identity only: it does not say the different P'_z form a compatible family. Nor does it turn arbitrary mixed cap restrictions into one common family of ambient halfspaces with the original labels. In particular the prefactor H/|N| in (4) need not be common across bases.

## 3. An actual exact obstruction at three consecutive labels

Take n=1,d=2 and the actual canonical product body

    C=[−1,1]_z × [0,1]_s × [−2,0]_t,
    P={−1,0,1}.

The common exposed contact plane is t=0. All three face fibers are the unit interval in s. Use the affine interior source graph y_z=(1/2,−1), so H_z=1, and the globally positive chart

    L(z,s,t)=1+z/2.

At the source base 0 the continuous parameter a=0 is indeed the ordinary centroid-normalizing parameter. The chosen base coefficient b=1/2 is an admissible positive extension; no assertion that it is the energy-supergradient choice is needed.

The weighted face masses (1) are exactly

    ν_(−1)=4,    ν_0=1,    ν_1=4/9.                   (6)

If these were the intrinsic one-dimensional volumes of ANY actual compatible convex family at these labels, its interval lengths would satisfy

    ν_0 ≥ (ν_(−1)+ν_1)/2 =20/9,

contrary to (6). Translations, shape changes, and nonlinear label-preserving transports cannot repair this volume obstruction. A unimodular change of the one-dimensional base merely reverses and translates the three labels and leaves their midpoint relation unchanged.

There is a stronger version. Suppose the same masses, up to any COMMON positive factor, were volumes of compatible convex fibers of an arbitrary finite positive continuous dimension r. Brunn–Minkowski would give

    1 ≥ [4^(1/r)+(4/9)^(1/r)]/2.

This is false for every r>0: the function z↦(1+z/2)^(−2/r) has strictly positive second derivative on [−1,1]. Thus no finite-dimensional uniform convex lift or positive concave-roof representation with these exact fiber totals and the same labels can exist. A pointwise convex roof lift would in particular give such total-volume fibers, so is excluded as well.

The homogenized chart does preserve ordinary convexity, but here it sends the labels −1,0,1 to −2,0,2/3. In (3), a_T=0 and s=L, so the image face lengths are 2,1,2/3, and their image support heights are also 2,1,2/3. Their products give exactly (6); replacing those products by intrinsic face lengths drops a real factor. The example is not an OC counterexample and does not concern a deepest-source selection. It disproves the proposed exact representation before any depth inference.

## 4. The inverse-power class that does survive

For m=d−1≥1, the density f=H L^(−m−1) on the flattened common face has

    f^(−1/m)=H (L/H)^((m+1)/m).                        (7)

This is convex jointly in (z,ξ): the function t↦t^((m+1)/m) is convex for t>0, and its perspective (H,L)↦H(L/H)^((m+1)/m) is convex for H>0. Composition with the actual affine H,L proves (7). Zero values outside the convex face support are understood as absent points, not as positive values to which this formula is applied.

There is a direct exact marginal stability statement. If f is bounded and positive continuous on a bounded open convex support and f^(−1/β) is convex for β>1, integrating ONE continuous coordinate gives a density whose inverse (β−1)-st power is convex on its positive support. At β=1 the marginal is quasiconcave. Iterating from (7), integrating r<m continuous coordinates leaves exponent −1/(m−r); integrating all m leaves only quasiconcavity in the remaining real base variables. No discrete summation is part of this assertion.

Here is a self-contained one-coordinate proof. At two remaining-coordinate points let the positive section masses be F_0,F_1 and their normalized increasing conditional quantiles X_i(s), 0<s<1. Their derivatives are X_i'=F_i/f_i, where f_i=f(z_i,X_i(s)). For z_λ=(1−λ)z_0+λz_1 put X_λ=(1−λ)X_0+λX_1. Convexity of the support and of f^(−1/β) gives, with u_i=f_i^(−1/β),

    f(z_λ,X_λ) ≥ [(1−λ)u_0+λu_1]^(−β),
    X_λ'=(1−λ)F_0 u_0^β+λF_1 u_1^β.

For β>1 weighted Hölder gives

    [(1−λ)u_0+λu_1]^β
      ≤ [(1−λ)F_0u_0^β+λF_1u_1^β]
        [(1−λ)F_0^(−1/(β−1))+λF_1^(−1/(β−1))]^(β−1).

The interpolated quantile interval lies in the actual intermediate section. Integrating the resulting lower bound on f(z_λ,X_λ)X_λ' proves the claimed inverse-power convexity. At β=1 the quotient is a weighted average of F_0,F_1 and is at least their minimum, proving quasiconcavity. The derivatives are valid on the open quantile interval because the densities are positive and continuous there; endpoint limits are handled by monotone exhaustion. Successive marginals are continuous on the interior of their convex positive supports, by section compactness and local dominated convergence, so the proof iterates. Initial contact densities are bounded on their compact supports.

If H is constant, the sharper initial exponent β=m+1 is available directly since f^(−1/(m+1)) is a positive multiple of L. Integrating all m continuous coordinates then leaves an inverse-first-power convex marginal. This still does not imply a positive root is concave; the calibration (6) already lies in this subclass.

## 5. Exact scope of the bridge

The actual full geometric contact face remains a genuine lower-dimensional mixed body with its unweighted intrinsic measure. Its projective boundary weight has the exact fiberwise cone-volume representation (4)–(5) and the stable ordinary inverse-power class (7). These are valid tools for continuous integrations and for tracking actual weighted traces.

The weighted totals cannot in general be replaced by uniform volumes of any compatible family at the old lattice labels. Ordinary projective convexity changes those labels, while arbitrary label-preserving transports cannot evade (6). The surviving negative-power class has a weaker marginal inequality, not the Brunn–Minkowski volume concavity required by the proposed convex lift. Proving a mixed statement for it would require a separate geometric argument; none is assumed here. Inward versus closed face traces and shared contact capacities from the archived contact-transport sources also remain separate obligations.
